flags.stem_preview: After the flood, Noah sent a bird out from the ark three times to see if dry land had appeared. The third time the bird returned with an olive leaf...
flags.issue: Factual error: stem says 'third time the bird returned with an olive leaf' but Genesis 8:8-12 has the dove return with olive leaf on its SECOND trip out, and NOT return at all on the third. The bank's own context field correctly states this. Stem and context contradict each other.
flags.suggested_fix: Reword stem: 'Noah sent the dove out three times: the second time it returned with an olive leaf in its beak; the third it did not return at all.' Then ask 'What kind of bird?'

flags.stem_preview: An Israelite judge had supernatural strength as long as his hair was never cut. His Philistine wife Delilah tricked him into revealing his secret...
flags.issue: Factual error: Delilah was Samson's lover (Judges 16:4 'a woman in the valley of Sorek, whose name was Delilah'), not his wife. Samson's only wife was the unnamed Philistine bride from Timnah (Judges 14). Other questions in this bank (#79, #133) get this right.
flags.suggested_fix: Change 'His Philistine wife Delilah' to 'A Philistine woman named Delilah' or 'His Philistine lover Delilah'.

flags.stem_preview: King David saw a beautiful woman bathing on a rooftop and arranged for her husband to be killed in battle so he could marry her...
flags.issue: Factual error: 2 Samuel 11:2 puts DAVID on his palace roof, not Bathsheba. She was visible from his roof (likely bathing in her courtyard). #83, #125 phrase this correctly; #21 and #765 share this error.
flags.suggested_fix: Change to 'King David, from the roof of his palace, saw a beautiful woman bathing below' or remove 'on a rooftop'.

flags.stem_preview: Mary and Joseph traveled to Bethlehem because of a Roman census. There was no room at the inn, so Mary gave birth to Jesus and laid him in a what?
flags.answer_preview: A manger (a feeding trough for animals)
flags.issue: TWO issues. (1) Stance violation: Context ends 'Bethlehem... fulfilling the prophecy of Micah.' This is the EXACT banned Christian-doctrinal framing per THEOLOGY_FRAMEWORK §5. The user is not Christian. (2) Choice-shape parity skim-tell: only correct answer has explanatory parens '(a feeding trough for animals)'; distractors are clean phrases.
flags.suggested_fix: (1) Change context to 'Bethlehem was the town of King David's birth; Matthew's Gospel ties this to Micah 5:2.' Drop 'fulfilling the prophecy'. (2) Drop the parens gloss — 'A manger' alone is the answer kids will recognize.

flags.stem_preview: Wise men from the East followed a star to Bethlehem to find the newborn king. They brought him three gifts...
flags.issue: Stance violation: Context ends 'myrrh — a burial spice — foreshadowed Jesus's death.' Unattributed Christian-doctrinal foreshadowing per THEOLOGY_FRAMEWORK §5. The symmetric-voice test fails: we don't write 'the mistletoe foreshadowed Ragnarok' in Norse questions.
flags.suggested_fix: Change to 'myrrh — used as a burial spice — was later read by Christian tradition as pointing to his death.' Or simply drop the foreshadowing.

flags.stem_preview: God tested Abraham's faith by ordering him to take his only son Isaac, climb a mountain in the land of Moriah, and offer him as a burnt sacrifice...

Attribution to 'Christians' softens this, but the bank consistently gives Christian readings of OT events without symmetric Norse/Greek parallels. Also uses devotional capitalization ('His own Son') for Jesus.
flags.suggested_fix: Rewrite as 'Christian readers have long interpreted Isaac on the wood as a parallel to Jesus carrying the cross to Golgotha.' Drop devotional capitalization.

flags.stem_preview: Odin's wife was the queen of Asgard and the goddess of marriage. She wept golden tears for the death of her beloved son Balder. Who was she?
flags.issue: Factual conflation: Frigg weeps for Balder in the Eddas, but 'golden tears' / 'tears of red gold' is FREYJA's trademark (weeping tears of gold for her absent husband Od). The 'golden tears' detail is being misattributed to Frigg, which is exactly the kind of Frigg-Freyja confusion T1 should avoid.
flags.suggested_fix: Change to 'She wept for her son Balder when he was killed by mistletoe' or 'She traveled the nine worlds extracting promises that nothing would harm her son'. Save 'golden tears' for a Freyja question.

flags.stem_preview: Three days of the English week are still named after Norse gods. Tuesday is the day of Tyr. Thursday is the day of Thor. Friday is the day of which Norse goddess?
flags.issue: Context hedge: 'Some scholars argue Friday is Freyja's day rather than Frigg's; the two were often confused in later Germanic tradition.' Scholarly consensus actually points to Frigg (Old English 'Frigedæg'); the hedge creates uncertainty for a tier-1 fact.
flags.suggested_fix: Either drop the Freyja/Frigg ambiguity context or tighten to 'Friday derives from Old English Frigedæg, named for Frigg.'
